clinicalPearls: A recessive enzyme defect that, unusually among glycolytic disorders, characteristically does not cause haemolytic anaemia
Deficiency of the muscle (M/A) subunit produces exercise intolerance and exertional myoglobinuria, resembling a glycogenoses-type myopathy
A dermatological phenotype with erythematosquamous skin lesions has been described with M-subunit deficiency
The subunit composition differs between tissues, so red cells tolerate the defect while muscle does not, explaining the paradoxical absence of haemolysis
A characteristic laboratory clue is a very low or absent serum LDH activity, which may be an incidental finding on routine biochemistry
Diagnosis is confirmed by isoenzyme analysis and enzyme assay, with LDHA or LDHB mutation testing
Management centres on avoiding the strenuous exertion that provokes rhabdomyolysis; specific treatment for the red cell is not required as haemolysis is absent
reference.pathophysiology: Lactate dehydrogenase interconverts pyruvate and lactate, regenerating the NAD+ needed to sustain anaerobic glycolysis under conditions of high energy demand. The enzyme is a tetramer of M (A) and H (B) subunits combined in tissue-specific ratios. In the red cell, alternative routes for NAD+ regeneration mean that deficiency does not appreciably shorten survival, so haemolysis is characteristically absent; in skeletal muscle, however, loss of the M subunit impairs anaerobic energy supply during exertion and predisposes to cramps, exercise intolerance and rhabdomyolysis.
additionalDifferentials: McArdle disease and other glycogen storage myopathies
Fatty-acid oxidation disorders causing exertional rhabdomyolysis
Analytical interference causing a spuriously low LDH
additionalInvestigations: Serum and red-cell lactate dehydrogenase activity with isoenzyme analysis
Forearm ischaemic exercise test assessing the lactate response
Creatine kinase and myoglobin during exertional symptoms
Full blood count and blood film to confirm the absence of haemolysis
Skin assessment for the associated erythematosquamous lesions
Molecular testing of the LDHA or LDHB genes
redFlags: Exertional rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria and risk of acute kidney injury
Recurrent disabling muscle cramps limiting activity
Extensive or ulcerating skin lesions requiring dermatological input
Pregnancy complications reported in M-subunit deficiency
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally good; because haemolysis is absent, morbidity relates to muscle symptoms and skin involvement, which are usually manageable with avoidance of heavy exertion.
pitfalls: Expecting a haemolytic anaemia and being misled when it is absent
Dismissing an incidentally low serum LDH as artefact without considering the diagnosis
Not testing the lactate response to exercise in a patient with exertional symptoms
